item.title: United States and Zambia Sign Five-Year Global Health Partnership under the Trump Administration’s America First Global Health Strategy
item.dc:creator: Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman
item.description:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman

United States and Zambia Sign Five-Year Global Health Partnership under the Trump Administration’s America First Global Health Strategy 

Press Statement

October 8, 2026

The United States and the Republic of Zambia today signed a five-year bilateral Health Cooperation Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) under the Trump Administration’s America First Global Health Strategy (AFGHS), a new model of health partnership built around greater Zambian investment, stronger accountability, and a clear path toward self-reliance. 

Building on more than 50 years of U.S. health assistance to Zambia, this MOU represents a $2.49 billion partnership of $1.52 billion in planned U.S. health assistance and a commitment from Zambia to invest $975 million in new funding in its own health system over five years. Under this MOU, the United States also plans to provide more than $13 million in Global Health Security funding to strengthen Zambia’s ability to detect and respond to infectious disease threats. Over five years, Zambia will progressively assume greater responsibility for its health system, including the procurement of health commodities, transitioning U.S.-supported frontline health workers into its civil service, and strengthening systems to track medicines and supplies from production to delivery. 

The United States will support Zambia in modernizing its health infrastructure, to include expanding electronic medical records and interoperable data systems for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and disease outbreak surveillance. 

The America First Global Health Strategy Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) signed to date represent more than $27.2 billion in new health funding, including more than $16.1 billion in U.S. assistance alongside more than $11.1 billion in co-investment from recipient countries, building on decades of progress fighting HIV/AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis, and other infectious diseases around the world. As of October 8, the State Department has signed 36 bilateral global health MOUs with Angola, Bolivia, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cambodia, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Guatemala, Guinea, Honduras, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Panama, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Rwanda, Senegal, Sierra Leone, South Sudan, Tajikistan, Tanzania, Uganda, Vietnam, and Zambia.

Secretary Rubio’s Meeting with Greek Prime Minister Mitsotakis

Readout

October 8, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis today, advancing our vital partnership with Greece.  They discussed expanding U.S.-Greece energy cooperation, reaffirmed deepening defense ties and regional security issues.  They committed to close cooperation to defeat transnational criminal organizations and safeguard critical infrastructure from emerging threats.

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Athens, Greece

Athens International Airport

Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press

Remarks

October 8, 2026

QUESTION:  Are you asking your allies to follow America First policy or to find their own path?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, I’m asking our allies to be strong.  The stronger they are, the stronger we are collectively.  That’s always been the theme.  We want a strong Europe.  We want strong partners in Europe.  We have – every country is different.  Obviously, they’re making different decisions.  But for example, in Greece, in Portugal where we’re going today, there are many countries that have stepped up – frankly, the Germans – who are stepping up and doing their part to be stronger.

The stronger – it’s a very simple concept.  It’s not very complicated, guys.  NATO is a collection of countries that have created an alliance.  The stronger the individual members of NATO are – both societally, economically, and militarily – the stronger NATO is.  And that’s what we want, and that’s what we’ve been asking for.  And I think there’s good signs in a lot of different places where that’s happening.  And obviously, there are some countries that are dragging, and I know they have a lot of domestic pressure, but I think this is good for all of us.

QUESTION:  On the reporting about your ambassador —

QUESTION:  Is there anything you wanted to – the reporting from The Wall Street Journal that Ambassador Guilfoyle had sought financial —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, guys, let me tell you something, okay?  You guys are going to ask me this.  You’re going to ask me again in Portugal.  I know the game, okay?  The game is someone gives information to a newspaper or a media outlet; the media outlet reports it.  You immediately turn to me and say, I need you to respond to our reporting.  That’s not the way this process works.  Like, our job is not to respond every time someone decides to give the media something without any advance warning, without having any chance to look at it and see what’s in there.  That’s not the way – that’s not the way you run an organization, and that’s not a serious way to conduct the policy of our country. 

So I’m not going to comment on a story that literally posted a few hours ago.  I get the game, okay?  I’ve been in this for a long time.  Within hours, some member of Congress will write you a letter demanding you answer questions to something we’ve never seen before.  I don’t even know if it’s true or not true.  So it’s just not going to work that way, and it most certainly is not going to work that way when I’m sitting in another country.  All right? 

QUESTION:  The speech last night, Mr. Secretary —

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, doesn’t that demand an – at the very least an IG investigation?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I am – guys, I’m not playing this game with you, okay?  You guys write a story and then your editors tell you, make sure you get a comment from him on something we haven’t seen, okay?  You guys are not going to be our only source of information in the world.  I’m sorry to tell you that.  And so I want you to understand —

QUESTION:  (Inaudible.)

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, that’s not the way the process is going to work. 

QUESTION:  How does the process work then?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, first of all, the process doesn’t work like this.  We don’t conduct these things in a press conference on a tarmac in a foreign country because you wrote a story or somebody else wrote a story because some source gave it to you.  So get that out of your head, because that’s never the way it’s going to work with me.  It’s a game that’s been played for a long time, but it’s not a game we’re going to play.  We’re conducting serious business here and we’ll handle things appropriately.  I don’t even know if what you’re reporting is true.  You guys somehow walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel.  It’s not the gospel.  It’s not the gospel for me.  That’s not the way we do it. 

QUESTION:  What are your feelings as you leave Greece, sir?

QUESTION:  On your speech, why did you – why did you feel like it was important right now to deliver the message you did last night?  Can you talk about the timing of the speech?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, it’s a consistent message.  I mean, the setting obviously is very unique because this is where democracy began.  This was where so many of the pillars and the foundations of the West are from.  And so it was a very unique setting obviously, and an opportunity to do it.  But I think in many ways it also, I think, reinforces our ties to Greece, which is really a model ally, and we wanted to make sure that came across as well. 

QUESTION:  Are Iranian threats constraining where the U.S. can operate in Europe and within NATO territory? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No.  The United States has the ability to operate – there’s nothing we – there is nothing we want or need to do against Iran that we can’t still do. 

QUESTION:  Can you compare and contrast Portugal and its support for the Iran operation with that of its immediate neighbor, Spain?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Can I compare and contrast it? 

QUESTION:  Or —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  That’s not the purpose.  The purpose of our visit is not to start a problem with another country.  Portugal is a great ally, a very cooperative ally of the United States, a country with which we already have a solid and growing relationship.  And we visit these countries in order to reinforce those ties.  That’s the purpose of the trip. 

QUESTION:  Okay, thank you.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  All right, let’s go home.  Well, not yet.  We’ve got to stop in Portugal.

QUESTION:  All right.  Thank you.

item.title: Designation of Fijian Resident for Involvement in Significant Corruption on Behalf of China-Based Actors
item.dc:creator: Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman
item.description:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman

Designation of Fijian Resident for Involvement in Significant Corruption on Behalf of China-Based Actors

Press Statement

October 7, 2026

Today, the Department of State is publicly designating Zhao Fugang, the Director of the Overseas Chinese Service Center located in Fiji, for his involvement in significant corruption on behalf of China-based actors.  This action renders Zhao and his immediate family members generally ineligible for entry into the United States.

Zhao abused his public position by paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance China-based government, business, and criminal interests.  His actions constituted significant corruption and adversely affected U.S. interests in Fiji.

The United States will hold accountable those who abuse power for personal gain, and continue to fight corruption that fuels drug trafficking, enables transnational criminal organizations, and threatens U.S. interests around the world.

These public designations are made under the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026 (Div. F, P.L. 119-75)(“Section 7031(c)”).  Section 7031(c) requires the Secretary of State to publicly or privately designate foreign officials and their immediate family members about whom the Secretary has credible information of involvement in significant corruption or a gross violation of human rights.

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis before their Expanded Meeting
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, Prime Minister
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Kyriakos Mitsotakis, Prime Minister

Athens, Greece

Maximos Mansion

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis before their Expanded Meeting

Remarks

October 7, 2026

PRIME MINISTER MITSOTAKIS:  We kept him a little bit longer, but it was a very, very good, productive discussion.  So let me welcome again, also, the whole team, and thank you also for the excellent preparation for the strategic dialogue.  I think we’ve made great progress, and we’re very, very happy to build upon a relationship that seems to be going from strength to strength.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, thank you.  It’s an honor to be here with you and your team.  We spent a lot of time together.  And we have in the past as well, and there’s so much that aligns us.  We’ve talked about it repeatedly today throughout our events, but we have a very unique historic alliance that has only grown, and now has the opportunity to grow even further – not just in the defense realm, where you’re a model ally, but when it comes to energy, economics, rare and critical minerals, supply chains.  I mean, you name it, the opportunities are extraordinary.  Energy is obviously a priority, and you’re a great partner on.

And so we value this relationship very much.  And I hope that today’s meeting and the strategic dialogue just continues to reaffirm it.  And we leave with – from these meetings always with action items that we follow up on to continue to build our relationship and strengthen it.

item.title: Joint Statement on the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

Joint Statement on the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue

Media Note

October 7, 2026

The following is the text of a joint statement by the United States of America and the Hellenic Republic on the occasion of the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue.

Begin text:

On October 7, 2026, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Minister of Foreign Affairs George Gerapetritis presided over the 6th round of the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue and held discussions on a wide area of global issues.  The two sides reaffirmed their steadfast, long and deep bilateral relations in the context of shared democratic values and Greece’s role as an active NATO ally.  Anchoring their discussions in shared priorities, both sides committed to deepen defense ties, bolster trade and investment, and promote cultural ties.

DEFENSE AND SECURITY COOPERATION

Greece and the United States reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthen their longstanding defense and security cooperation.  The United States and Greece announced $4 billion in Foreign Military Sales in support of Greece’s long-term defense plan to deepen our interoperability, and to explore future opportunities for defense industrial base cooperation, including on innovative technologies.  They finalized Greece’s participation in the U.S. National Guard Bureau’s State Partnership Program with Florida, and enhanced interoperability through the provision of Stryker vehicles to Greece.  Both sides reaffirmed the strategic value of our defense cooperation in support of bilateral and NATO security objectives.  They expanded law enforcement and counterterrorism cooperation and reaffirmed their commitment to address illegal migration.

ECONOMIC AND TRADE COOPERATION

Greece and the United States reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening two-way trade and investment.  They recognized the importance of economic security and intend to partner to strengthen investment screening and protect critical infrastructure procurements.  With Greece’s status as a Pax Silica signatory, the two sides welcomed growing cooperation in super intelligence, high-performance computing, cybersecurity, and advanced technologies.  They highlighted deepening energy ties, building on the November 2025 P-TEC ministerial, the Vertical Gas Corridor, and hydrocarbon exploration.  They underscored the significance of maritime collaboration and signed an agreement on certification for U.S. seafarers on Greek vessels.

CULTURAL TIES 

The governments also signed an extension of their Cultural Property Agreement, reaffirming their commitment to protect cultural heritage and combat illicit trafficking networks.  In addition, they announced the United States’ first project in Greece under the Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation to highlight shared democratic traditions.

End Text.

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis at a Joint Press Availability
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State, Giorgos Gerapetritis, Greek Foreign Minister
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Giorgos Gerapetritis, Greek Foreign Minister

Athens, Greece

Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis at a Joint Press Availability

Remarks

October 7, 2026

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  (In Greek.) 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.  Thank you for your welcome.  It’s actually great to be here to have our sixth Strategic Dialogue, which is ongoing, and we’ve begun downstairs a few minutes ago.  It’s an event where our two countries commit to continue to work together on a range of issues. 

We are two countries that are bound by a common heritage and by proud histories.  The United States and Greece share a long history of friendship and partnership and alliance.  In fact, the importance of this historical alliance is highlighted by the instability in the world today that we see as a result of conflicts in Hormuz with Iran, or the conflicts in the Red Sea with – in Yemen, or the conflicts in Ukraine and Russia.  As you see a world that faces these destabilizing events, you recognize how important this alliance with Greece is to the United States. 

It’s both historic – historical in its foundation, but it is also critical.  It is a source of stability in an unstable world.  And I’m thankful – we’re thankful – that Greece remains a great ally and that we share a common understanding – this is really important – not just a great ally – we share a common understanding of the threats that face our countries, the face – the threat – that face our societies.  And we share a common understanding about the means to address them. 

One thing we agree on, for example, is that the nations of Europe need to take on a greater share of the burden in defending their continent, and Greece is doing just that.  They’re on track to meet the commitments that have been made to spend 5 percent of their GDP on defense this year, with over 3.5 of that – of their GDP – percent of GDP being spent on core defense.  They’re also joining the National Guard’s Bureau of State Partnership Program, and they’ll be paired, ironically enough, with the Florida National Guard, which will bring our military collaboration even closer. 

Greece is also very close strategic partner on border security in the fight against mass migration, against fighting – they’re a great ally as well on fighting transnational criminal organizations, on counterterrorism.  Due to its geography in the Mediterranean at the crossroads of many of these transit routes, Greece is particularly exposed to the threats posed by mass migration, by human trafficking, by different forms of terror. 

Now, as part of our efforts to combat these common threats to our nations, we’re proud to announce a new Memorandum of Understanding establishing a joint security program to strengthen the counterterrorism information sharing between our respective law enforcement agencies.  What we do not wish to see under any circumstances is that the birthplace of the West is threatened by bad decisions, by inactions, by failure to address challenges.  And so, this program is going to create stronger, more proactive law enforcement cooperation that could readily stop these threats.

As I was already mentioned, Greece is already a major player in the Red Sea operation under the (inaudible) of the European Union, the speediest operation for the safe navigation of vessels passed through the Red Sea.  If it is necessary to participate in additional operations and a framework of greater cooperation that will be (inaudible) passage from the Gulf, it is obvious that Greece will once again be at the forefront.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  What was your first question?

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the U.S. Embassy Chancery Dedication Ceremony
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Athens, Greece

U.S. Embassy

Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the U.S. Embassy Chancery Dedication Ceremony

Remarks

October 7, 2026

AMBASSADOR GUILFOYLE:  Kalimera.  Secretary Rubio, Your Grace Bishop (inaudible), colleagues from Washington and from this mission, good afternoon.  Today is truly a special day for the United States Embassy in Greece as we inaugurate our new chancellor.  In a country where the history of democracy lies beneath our feet, we are proud to dedicate this new building where we work hard every day on behalf of the American people.  This ceremony dedicates a building, but it also renews our purpose to advance American interests, protect American lives, and strengthen our alliance.

There is no greater honor than to open this new chapter in American diplomacy with our 72nd Secretary of State and National Security Advisor – and my dear friend – Marco Rubio.  Secretary Rubio is a true friend of Greece, and he is a champion of democracy.  Throughout his distinguished career, he has stood shoulder to shoulder with our allies to defend liberty across the globe.  His visit today shows that the United States-Greece partnership is more vibrant and more vital than ever.  Secretary Rubio has been the strongest and the most steadfast supporter of this important relationship for many, many years, going back to his days in the Senate.  It is only fitting that he is here to commemorate this historic moment in the history of the United States Diplomatic Mission to Greece.

I am also deeply touched that His Grace the Bishop Theofilestatos Varnavas has joined us today.  The Greek Orthodox Church plays an extraordinary role in the spiritual life of both the United States and Greece.  Your presence reminds us that everything we do at this mission serves a higher purpose.  I now invite His Grace to offer a blessing, followed by remarks from Secretary Rubio.  Thank you, God bless you, God bless Greece, and may God bless the United States of America.

(The blessing was made.)

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I didn’t want to hurt anyone.  (Laughter.)  I’m going after (inaudible).  How am I supposed to follow that?  (Laughter.)  Thank you, (inaudible).  Thank you so much.  Thank you, Your Grace, for this.  Thank you, Ambassador, for hosting.  Thank you all for being here.  It’s – this is one of the Department of State’s most impressive and historic embassies.  (Inaudible) to engage in diplomacy with one of our key allies in the world, and I want to thank all of you for doing this, and thank you again for blessing this new workplace.  I also want to recognize the five American public servants who have died in the line of duty, victims of the brutal reign of violence of (inaudible) terrorist groups. 

Our embassies are more than just buildings.  They’re architectural reflections of our country.  I mean, that is the first impression that we make in many cases on our host nation.  But they also have (inaudible) functional.  They should keep the staff inside safe, and they should secure the sensitive documents and the conversations that protect American citizens wherever they are in the world. 

But stylistically, when appropriate, they should be designed in a uniquely American way.  They should show strength.  They should show leadership and an openness to engagement.  And this embassy with this marble – it’s the same marble that was used to build the Parthenon – reflects our cultural ties to the region and our reverence for the city’s history and influence on our own nation’s institutions.  The completion of these renovations renews that acknowledgement for the ties we share with this land, and also to the high esteem in which we hold the city’s great monuments.

But of course, an embassy is just an empty building without the contents.  The completion of these renovations at last bring back together all the embassy staff who have been held at other locations during the years of the construction.  Many of you have been offsite for (inaudible) years now, and we in the Department are grateful for your flexibility and your patience during this prolonged process. 

I’m very proud to be the Secretary to participate in the ribbon-cutting ceremony, and I hope that this building will continue to foster the strong relations between the United States and our host nation, Greece.  And just as the Parthenon inspired your architect’s design of this building over 60 years ago, may the history, artifacts, and (inaudible) ruins of the city’s ancient civilization inspire us to remember – and never to forget – our proud Western heritage and values as we conduct our work here.  So, thank you.  (Applause.)

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis at the Opening Session of the United States-Greece Strategic Dialogue
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State, Giorgos Gerapetritis, Greek Foreign Minister
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Giorgos Gerapetritis, Greek Foreign Minister

Athens, Greece

Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis at the Opening Session of the United States-Greece Strategic Dialogue

Remarks

October 7, 2026

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  Dear Secretary, dear colleagues, it is a great pleasure to welcome and your delegation to Athens for the sixth round of the Greece-U.S. Strategic Dialogue.  Your presence here speaks to the enduring strength of our relationship and to the importance both our countries attach to its future.   

Since the launch of the Strategic Dialogue back in 2018, our cooperation has grown steadily in scope and ambition, encompassing defense, energy, infrastructure, digital technologies, law enforcement, maritime affairs, and the close ties between our peoples.  The three agreements signed today are tangible evidence of that progress.  Our partnership has never been stronger, deeper, or more consequential.  It rests on shared values and a common determination to advance peace, stability, security, and prosperity for our peoples, for our regions, and beyond.   

We meet at a time of profound geopolitical change.  The ongoing war in Ukraine, instability in the Middle East, threats to maritime security in the Red Sea, and the resurgence of a revisionist rhetoric demand resolve, coordination, and a clear sense of purpose.  In this uncertain environment, Greece remains a reliable ally and an anchor of stability in the Eastern Mediterranean.  During the 2025-‘26 term on the United Nations – of the Security Council – and as we prepare to assume the presidency of the Council of the European Union second semester of 2027 – we bring that same sense of responsibility to our work.  Respect for international law is a guiding principle for our foreign policy and an essential condition for lasting peace.   

Greece’s geography places us at the meeting point of three continents.  Our history, our longstanding relationships across the region, and the enduring influence of Hellenism allow us to engage with a wide range of partners in good faith and with credibility.  This gives Greece a particular responsibility and a practical capacity to connect countries, facilitate dialogue, and build understanding.  It also gives our partnership strategic value.  Strengthening Greece’s role strengthens the security of the wider region and advances interests we share with the United States.   

The Strategic Dialogue allow us to translate this convergence into concrete action.  Today, we have an opportunity to carry that world forward across its core pillars.  Our defense cooperation has reached unprecedented levels.  The Mutual Defense Cooperation Agreement has deepened our strategic partnership and strengthened our capacity to address common security challenges.   

Alexandroupolis exemplifies the value of this cooperation.  A sovereign Greek port and a vital logistical hub for the United States, it contributes directly to the security of nations – of NATO’s eastern flank.  Greece’s consistently high defense expenditure and longstanding contribution to the Alliance reflect a simple conviction:  Collective security requires every Ally to shoulder its responsibilities.  We are committed to further strengthening our defense cooperation, including through procurement, industrial partnerships, and advanced technologies.  Our growing collaboration in law enforcement and counterterrorism is equally important to the security of our citizens.   

On energy, Greece is emerging as a vital hub for Southeastern and Central Europe infrastructure, such as the Alexandroupolis FSRU.  Together with our leading role in the Vertical Corridor, this diversifying supply is strengthening resilience and giving our neighbors greater energy security.  The growing engagement of U.S. energy companies, including Severn and ExxonMobil, underscores confidence, increases potential, (inaudible) the opportunities our partnership offers.   

Our maritime strength are the third strategic dimension.  With Greek-owned vessels accounting for almost one-fourth of global energy shipping capacity globally, Greek shipping plays a pivotal role in connecting energy producers with consumers and sustaining transatlantic energy flows.  The transformation of the Greek economy has opened a new chapter in our bilateral relationship.  Renewed growth and investment confidence are creating opportunities for American businesses to participate in Greece’s progress.   

Investment by leading U.S. technology companies in data centers’ digital infrastructure is helping to establish Greece as a regional center for innovation.  Our ambition is to build on this momentum through partnerships that create skilled jobs, support research, and bring new opportunities to the next generation.   

At the heart of this relationship, however, are our people.  The Greek American community has helped shape America while sustaining a close and abiding connection with Greece.  Its achievements in business, science, public service, and the arts are a source of pride for both our nations.  Greek Americans have made Greece’s heritage part of America’s success.  They embody a relationship rooted in the ideals of liberty, democracy, and the rule of law, ideals that inspired America’s Founding Fathers and continue to give our partnership purpose.  Our expanding education and cultural exchanges carry this connection forward, allowing young Greeks and Americans to learn from one another and to build relationships of their own.   

Mr. Secretary, I look forward to our discussions today and to the practical results that we deliver.  We have a strong foundation and a clear sense of what we can achieve.  Today’s discussion will help us turn that shared ambition into practical results.  Our alliance draws strength – draws strength from all we have achieved together.  Its promise lies in what we choose to do next.  Thank you. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, thank you.  Thank you for this opportunity to be here today for the sixth time a U.S. secretary of state gathers with their counterparts in Greece for this Strategic Dialogue.  And I’m happy to be here in Greece for that dialogue.  It’s my first trip to the country ever; I didn’t even have a chance to come as a senator.  And so I’m happy to be here and to be a part of this Strategic Dialogue.   

I want to begin by saying that I hope our presence here today and our work that we’re about to do – and continue to do together – highlights something very important, and that is how critical the historic alliance between Greece and the United States is.  And this is especially true now at a time of great global uncertainty, whether it’s the war between Russia and Ukraine, whether it’s what’s happening in the Middle East, whether it’s – meaning in the Straits of Hormuz and, increasingly now, in the Red Sea because of the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.   

At a time of extraordinary global tumult and global instability, we need anchor partners rooted in a common history.  And that is what Greece has meant for the United States and, I hope, what the United States has meant for Greece and what we will continue to mean for each other.  This strong partnership, it’s a relationship that spans a variety of fronts – obviously defense and security, our mutual defense and security as allies and partners, but it extends to trade, to investment, to energy.  There literally is no – it’s a cultural exchange.  There are literally no areas of our societies or of our countries that are not part of the U.S.-Greece relationship, and we seek to build and expand on every single one of them.   

Let me begin by saying what is obvious to everyone but should continue to be obvious:  Greece is an indispensable NATO partner, an indispensable NATO Ally.  It is a pillar of stability in this region, it is a pillar of the U.S.’s presence in this region, and it is a pillar of how we secure our national interest as well as Greece’s in the region.  So we are thrilled – part of that, some of the things that aren’t heavily perceived but we’ll be able to be a part of announcing again later today, is we’re thrilled that Greece joins the

U.S. National Guard Bureau of State Sponsorship Program, and they’re doing so with the guard from my home state of Florida.  It’s another milestone in our deepening defense relationship. 

The U.S.-Greece Economic Security Declaration commits both nations to continue to work with likeminded allies as well to develop secure supply chains.  That includes – including critical mineral productions, again another area of very strong cooperation in which our mutual interests are aligned but also in which we’re taking concrete action. 

Our energy relationship is reaching new heights, and it continues to expand and grow, and it’s something we’re going to be building on.  The Vertical Gas Corridor expansion has cemented in Greece, has cemented Greece as an energy hub and as a secure energy hub, and has facilitated increase in U.S. LNG exports to Europe.  That’s something we continue to build on. 

Our bilateral relationship as countries, of course, at the end, is founded not just in a common history but in enduring ties of family, of culture, of religion, of a shared heritage.  As I’ll speak about later today in what I think is a pretty historic setting, from what I read – (laughter) – it – we are indebted to ancient Greece for its role in shaping not just our country but, frankly, our civilization. 

And we – so we’re here today to remember the past because that’s the foundation upon which our relationship is built, but also to focus on the future, because we have incredible things that we can do together.  And I’m very grateful to be a part of this, to be – excited to be a part of the Strategic Dialogue and happy to be here on my first visit to Greece but hopefully not my last.

Partnership

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, thank you.  Thank you for this opportunity to be here today for the sixth time a U.S. secretary of state gathers with their counterparts in Greece for this Strategic Dialogue.  And I’m happy to be here in Greece for that dialogue.  It’s my first trip to the country ever; I didn’t even have a chance to come as a senator.  And so I’m happy to be here and to be a part of this Strategic Dialogue.

At a time of extraordinary global tumult and global instability, we need anchor partners rooted in a common history.  And that is what Greece has meant for the United States and, I hope, what the United States has meant for Greece and what we will continue to mean for each other.  This strong partnership, it’s a relationship that spans a variety of fronts – obviously defense and security, our mutual defense and security as allies and partners, but it extends to trade, to investment, to energy.  There literally is no – it’s a cultural exchange.  There are literally no areas of our societies or of our countries that are not part of the U.S.-Greece relationship, and we seek to build and expand on every single one of them.
